newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Mistake left police in Timor vunerable to attack.
newsitem.headline: Mistake left police in Timor vunerable to attack.

text.p: Indonesia's military on Sunday blamed the deaths of 17 troops in a separatist ambush in East Timor on an operational mistake that left them vulnerable to attack.

Major-General Abdul Rivai said the 16 policemen and one soldier, returning from a mission to provide election security, were killed after their lone truck was ambushed near Quelcai, about 130 km (80 miles) east of the capital Dili.

"It is standard procedure, including for election security units, that when returning from duty at least two vehicles should be used in order to protect each other from undesirable things," the official Antara news agency quoted Rivai, commander of the Udayana military region covering East Timor, as saying.
He said 13 of the victims died from burns and four were shot after a grenade was thrown into their truck, which had stopped to give a lift to a number of people wearing military uniforms.
Five others were seriously injured and six received light wounds, he added.
"Inside the Hino truck there was a barrel of petrol. After the truck exploded a number of people were shot after trying to escape from the rebels," Rivai said.
An army driver and co-driver were ferrying 26 policemen back to the territory's second city of Baucau on Saturday morning after they helped secure Thursday's general election when they were attacked.
Rivai said it was not known if there had been any casualties on the attackers' side.
Another 17 people died on Wednesday and Thursday during attacks by separatists trying to disrupt Indonesia's general elections, in which the ruling Golkar party won 74 percent of the vote.
Deputy East Timor police chief Colonel Atok Rismanto said earlier on Sunday there had been no other security problems in East Timor since the ambush and life was normal in Dili.
"Church services are going ahead, people are going to market and others are swimming at the beach," he said.

The ambush was part of the worst upsurge of violence in years in the territory, which Indonesia occupied in 1975 and annexed as its 27th province the following year. The United Nations has refused to recognise Indonesian sovereignty.

East Timor police chief Colonel Yusuf Muharam said on Saturday police had detained 22 suspects -- including 13 "rebels" and nine supporters -- in connection with an attack on a police station in Dili in which four rebels were killed on Wednesday night.
Twelve civilians and one soldier were shot in another three separate incidents.
One diplomatic source said it was unclear whether the latest ambush signalled a longer-term escalation of violence.

The Indonesian military, which maintains a strong presence in East Timor, says about 80 poorly armed guerrillas remain in the rugged hills in the territory. Other sources suggest there are around 200.
Jakarta officially has five full battalions of troops as well as other units in East Timor numbering around 5,000 men, far more than in neighbouring provinces with much larger populations.
